narrative:
Your application was denied because the model determined you have a 58 percent chance of being a bad credit risk—meaning that, based on people with similar profiles, you were seen as more likely to struggle with repaying the loan than to repay it reliably. That level of risk was too high for approval.

The single most important factor working against you was the condition of your checking account. Your account was overdrawn, with a negative balance. Among approved applicants, only a small minority had a negative balance; most had no overdraft or at least some positive funds. This strongly signaled financial strain and pushed the decision toward denial.

The second most influential factor actually helped you. You asked to borrow the money over only 12 months, which is shorter than the typical loan duration of about 19 months. A shorter repayment period usually suggests less time for things to go wrong, so this pointed toward you being a better risk. Unfortunately, it was not enough to overcome the concerns above.

The third most important factor was your property situation. You had no identifiable property or assets, such as real estate, a car, or a savings-related policy. Most approved applicants had at least some asset to show, so your lack of property added to the perception that you would have fewer resources to fall back on if your finances became difficult.

To improve your chances in the future, focus first on getting your checking account into positive territory and keeping it there. Building even a small savings cushion or acquiring any form of tangible asset would also help. After several months of stable account activity, you may be in a much stronger position to reapply.
